papers.title: Turning Old Anomalies Into New Evidence: Evidential Reconfiguration and Dark Matter in 1974
papers.abstract: The 1974 papers by Ostriker et al. (1974) and Einasto et al. (1974) are regarded as pivotal in establishing the evidential case for dark matter, although both relied on already existing observational data. By what means did they transform known observational anomalies into evidential support for dark matter? I argue that this transformation arose through evidential reconfiguration: extended galactic halos supplied a physical connection between galaxy rotation curves and cluster mass discrepancies, expanding the context of assessment so that results previously investigated locally could constrain one another. The significance of this connection was assessed against differing cosmological commitments and unresolved local dynamical assumptions, which help explain both the emphases of the two papers and their reception. To explicate its contribution to confirmation, I draw on Myrvold's Bayesian account of unification and use a toy model in which taking one result into account changes the assessment of a shared halo parameter, thereby altering expectations about the other. Comparison with an uncoupled model makes the resulting support explicit, while variations of the model show why a shared parameter alone is insufficient: the contribution depends on the connecting assumptions and what competing models predict. The novelty relevant to the old-evidence problem thus lies in what familiar observations became jointly capable of supporting. This reconstruction assesses that support once the connection is specified, while leaving a full account of historical belief change open.
